questions.q: What is the most straightforward data exfiltration pattern described in this lesson?
options: A single DNS query to a well-known public resolver
Traffic that uses TCP instead of UDP
An unusually large outbound transfer to an unfamiliar destination, often outside the host's normal active hours
Any traffic at all moving between two internal hosts
questions.explain: This pattern is exactly what a per-host traffic baseline is built to catch: an unusual volume, destination, and timing all at once.

questions.q: How does DNS tunneling hide stolen data?
options: By renaming files to have a .dns extension
By encoding it into the subdomain portion of DNS queries sent to an attacker-controlled domain
By encrypting the entire hard drive before transfer
By disabling DNS entirely on the compromised host
questions.explain: DNS tunneling exploits DNS's near-universal outbound allow rule by hiding encoded data inside query subdomains.

questions.q: What makes beaconing detectable, according to this lesson?
options: The suspiciously regular, periodic interval between check-ins, not necessarily the destination itself
Beaconing traffic is always encrypted with a known weak cipher
Beacons always transfer more than 1 GB per connection
Beacons only ever occur over port 80
questions.explain: The mechanical regularity of the check-in interval, visible across many flows over time, is the real tell.

questions.q: Why does a newly registered domain often get flagged as suspicious?
options: Newly registered domains are always technically invalid
It's a common indicator threat intelligence feeds use alongside other signals, since attacker infrastructure is often registered shortly before use
All newly registered domains are automatically blocked by every firewall
DNS cannot resolve any domain registered less than a year ago
questions.explain: A newly registered domain is one signal among several, not proof by itself, but it's commonly flagged in threat intelligence.

questions.q: In the chapter's combined exfiltration case, which signals together made the strongest case for compromise?
options: A baseline deviation, a beaconing interval, a newly registered destination, and DPI-confirmed DNS tunneling
An employee's badge access logs alone
The workstation's CPU temperature readings
A single large file transfer and nothing else
questions.explain: No single signal proved anything alone; it was the combination of flow, baseline, and DPI evidence that made the case strong.
